# Recovery of cobalt as cobalt oxalate from spent lithium ion batteries by using glycine as leaching agent

## ABSTRACT

In the article, we are explaining a hydrometallurgical based process on leaching applied to recover Co from spent lithium ion batteries (LIBs). Glycine and ascorbic acid were introduced as leaching reagents and the leaching of Co with a solution containing glycine is investigated. An effective recovery of Co is possible when both glycine and ascorbic acid are used. A condition for achieving a recovery of more than 95% Co has been achieved experimentally by varying the concentrations of leachant and time of the reaction. Leaching with 0.5 M glycine, 0.02 M ascorbic acid and 0.2 g LiCoO2 in a batch extractor, results in a highly efficient recovery of Co within 360 min of the processing time at 80 ^∘C. This hydrometallurgical process is found to be simple, eco friendly and satisfactory for the recovery of cobalt from spent LIBs. ã 2016 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

## 1. Introduction

Rechargeable lithium ion battery (LIB) is a device that meets certain crucial demands ofour modern society, acting as the power source of various portable devices like mobile phones, laptop computers, electric vehicles (EVs), hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) and grid level power systems [1]. Due to their high energy density, long lifespan, light weight and compatibility, they grab the attention of people. Sony made the first commercial lithium ion battery in 1991 [2] which substituted the other type of batteries. LIBs consisted of lithium-intercalating material as anode (typically graphitic carbon) and lithium metal oxides as cathode. LiCoO2 is the most used cathode material due to its good performance. With the development of these products, the numbers of secondary batteries have increased enormously. The higher number of LIBs uses means that a huge amount of spent LIBs have been generated worldwide [3]. On the other hand, the spent LIBs cannot be disposed off into the landfill owing to safety and economic reasons [4]. LIBs include of heavy metals, organic chemicals and plastics in the following proportions: 5–20% Co, 5–10% Ni, 5–7% Li, approximately 15% organic chemicals and 7% plastics which are higher than those found in natural ores [5–8]. In addition, spent LIBs also contain toxic and flammable organic electrolyte (LiBF and LiPF6 dissolved in organic solvent), which is well thought-out as both an attractive secondary resource and environmental pollutant [9,10]. At present, the main options for the treatment of spent LIBs are recycling, remanufacturing, reuse, and landfilling. In general, spent LIBs are discarded as domestic waste, which is environmentally unacceptable. Therefore recycling of these spent LIBs is considered to be beneficial to prevent environmental pollution.

Recycling processes of spent LIBs usually pretreat with physical separation techniques [11] such as mechanical, mechanochemical and thermal dissolution processes. Subsequently, battery components can be recovered through chemical separation techniques [12] such as acid leaching, bioleaching, chemical precipitation, solvent extraction and electrochemical processes. Hitherto, several approaches have been made to recycle LiCoO2 from the spent LIBs using strong inorganic and organic acids through pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy processes [13,10].

From previous studies, it has been found that the metals such as Co and Li can be leached out from the spent LIBs using inorganic acid such as HCl [9], H2S04 [14,15], HNO [16,17] and various organic acids such as ascorbic acid [18], citric acid [19,20], malic acid, aspartic acid [19] oxalic acid [21], -maleic acid [22], Succinic acid [23], tartaric acid [24] iminodiacetic acid and maleic acid [25] in the presence of H2O2 as well as ascorbic acid [ 20, 24, 25 ] ] as reducing agent. Here in all these studies, they have used H2O2 and ascorbic acid as reducing agent to increase the leaching efficiency. Table 1 summarizes the recent significant literature incorporating the relevant findings achieved on the leaching of metals using inorganic and organic acids from the spent LIBs.

[TABLE:TABLE_Recovery of Cobalt as Cobalt Oxalate from Spent Lithium Ion Batteries by Using Glycine as Leaching Agent_0001]

Even though there are many techniques which have been introduced to recycle valuable metals from spent LIBs, their economic and environmental compatibility is found to be less than satisfactory. Also, the leaching efficiency for valuable metals, such as Co and Li, is low and still needs to be improved. Therefore our aim is to develop the economically adequate and environmental benign recycling process i.e., to avoid the inorganic acids and to improve the leaching efficiency; we have used an aqueous mixture of glycine (leaching/chelating agent) and ascorbic acid (reductant).

In this study to recover metals from spent LIB active cathode material, we have chosen glycine as leaching agent because it is low cast compared to citric acid, tartaric acid iminodiacetic acid and maleic acid. As well it is a naturally occurring simplest amino acid, soluble easily in water and was frequently used as a raw material in the manufacturing industries. Also it is well-known to act as a complexing agent for metal ions as it has amino group at the one end and carboxylic acid group at the other end. The dipolar (zwitter) ionic nature of glycine molecule can efficiently complex a metal ion of diverse ionic sizes, whose structure protonates or deprotonates depending on the pH of solution [26]. As the acidity of solution decreases, the amount of unprotonated glycine increases and the intensity of the bands grow which confirms the formation of a complex species. The glycine is extensively used as a model compound for theoretical and experimental investigations dedicated to the elucidation of the interactions occurring between metal ions and biological systems in many life processes [27]. Here we used ascorbic acid as reducing agent (H2 A ⟶2 H ^+ + 2e + A) which is an environmentally benign and kinetically have been proved as a strong reductant in the dissolution studies of metal oxides [28].

The details on leaching behavior of LiCoO cathode material from a spent LIBs and the selective precipitation of constituent metals are reported here. Unlike using strong in-organic acids, the mild organic acids used here are advantageous in all respects like elimination of contamination and low damage to the experimental apparatus, as well as easy bio-degradation. As per the literature, the present study to dissolve LiCoO using is glycine as leaching chelating agent and ascorbic acid as reducing agent is an unexplored area of research.

## 2. Materials and methods

## 2.1. Materials and reagents

The spent LIBs ofBL-5CA (Nokia mobile) series used in this work were collected in the local market. The cathode material was separated from aluminum foil by using concentrated N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP). The leaching reagents used in this work consisted of glycine and ascorbic acid which were mild organic acids. The reagents used in this study were analytical grade, and all the solutions were prepared with known concentrations in distilled water.

## 2.2. Experimental

## 2.2.1. Dismantling and separation

To prevent self-ignition and short-circuiting, the spent LIBs were discharged completely and dismantled to separate the cathode and anode materials coated on Al- and Cu-foil, respectively. The cathode material was uncurled and cut in to small pieces (about 1 cm). These pieces were immersed in 100 mL concentrated NMP solvent and subjected for ultrasonic washing using ultrasonic bath (Model—SUG-321, S. No. 90933) at about 1 h. After ultrasonic washing the active cathode material was separated from Al - f o i l,, filtered and heated at 700 ^∘C for 2 h to burn off the organics such as carbon and polyvinylidene fluoride. The powder was then ground for 30 min to obtain smaller particles with higher surface to increase leaching efficiency. Fig. 1 shows the flow sheet of the process intended in this work. As reported in Figs. 2 and 3, the oxide thus obtained was found to be LiCoO2 based on XRD and SEM/EDX analysis. The rock salt structured LiCoO was found to contain residual carbon, 5–10 wt.%, due to organic burn off. The origin for such carbon might be from the acetylene black used to ensure the electronic conductivity in the cathodes.

## 2.2.2. Dissolution of LiCoO2 in mixture of glycine and ascorbic acid

The above cathode material (LiCoO2, 0.2: g) was subjected for chemical dissolution using mild organic acids, an aqueous mixture of glycine and ascorbic acid were taken in a three necked roundbottomed flask with volume of100 mL and the flask was placed in a water bath to control the reaction temperature during the leaching. The flask was fitted with vapor condenser and a magnetic stirrer. In the leaching process, the concentration of tartaric acid was varied (0.1–0.5 M) by keeping ascorbic acid concentration constant (0.02 M). After 6 h leaching at 80 ^∘𝖢,, the solution and insoluble residue were separated by filtration by using (0.2 mm) membrane filter paper and washed with distilled water, yielding a pink filtrate and a black residue.

## 2.3. Analytical methods

The concentration of Li and Co metal ions in the dissolved solution was determined by using atomic absorption spectrophotometer (Model: AA-7000F, ROM version: 1.01, S/N: A30664801195). The results obtained here were found to carry a maximum of about 5% error. UV–vis spectra of the dissolved solution was also recorded using UV–vis spectrophotometer (Ocean optics, DH-2000 BAL). X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern was obtained using Cu Ka radiation (λ = 1.542 A) with a Ni-filter (Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer). Morphology (SEM, HITACHI S-3000H) and the elemental composition of the sample were examined by recording energy dispersive _ X - r a y (EDXA) spectra. FT-IR spectrum was recorded on a Nicolet 5DX-FTIR spectroscopy with KBr pellet.

## 3. Results and discussion

## 3.1. Characterization of the LiCoO2 in spent LIBs

Fig. 2 shows the XRD patterns of spent LiCoO2 cathode material after calcinations and grinding. From XRD data, the crystalline LiCoO2 phase was clearly identified as rock–salt structured [20] and the main compositions of this spent cathode material are LiCoO2 and CoO. In general, the CoO present in the cathode material results from the transformation of LiCoO [29]. Fig. 3 shows SEM/EDX images of the spent LiCoO2 cathode material and the particles were irregularly agglomerated with approximate 5 - 10 μ m diameters. EDXA analysis shows the presence of Co (except Li which cannot be detected by EDXA). SEM/EDX analysis confirms the residual carbon present along with this cathode material due to organic burn off. The source for such carbon might be from the acetylene black used to make sure the electronic conductivity in the cathodes.

## 3.2. Effect of glycine concentration on leaching

The effect of glycine concentration on the leaching efficiency of waste LiCoO2 have been studied by varying concentration from

0.1 M to 0.5 M at temperature of 80 ^∘C for 6 h. The ascorbic acid (reductant) concentration used is 0.02 M and was kept constant. Fig. 4 shows the concentration dependency for leaching cobalt. The leaching efficiency of Co increases from 70% to 95% as the glycine concentration increases from 0.1 to 0.5 M. Therefore, here we used 0.5 M glycine with 0.02 M ascorbic acid for further leaching studies.

There are many studies on organic acid leaching. They have obtained more than 90% leaching of Co and about 100% leaching of Li in about 90–120 min by using 1.25 M citric acid [30], 1.5 M DL-malic acid [19], 1.0 M oxalic acid [31] along with H O as reducing agent. In all these studies they have used more concentrations to dissolve the metal ions completely, but in our case as reported in our previous study we have used mild concentrations; 0.1 M citric acid gives 80%, 0.4 M tartaric acid gives more than 90%, 0.1 M iminodiacetic acid gives 91% and 0.1 M maleic acid gives 97% Co and nearly 100% Li ions dissolution in the presence of 0.02 M ascorbic acid [20,24,25].

## 3.3. Leaching with glycine and ascorbic acid

Fig. 5 shows the percentage of Co ions released from LiCoO in glycine and ascorbic acid (0.02 M) mixture at 80 C for 6 h. Here, in leaching of waste LiCoO we have tried the dissolution for stoichiometric glycine and ascorbic acid ratio with respect to the cathode material used. We used 0.02 M metal ion worth of LiCoO2 sample and was added to 100 mL water containing 0.1 - 0.5 N glycine and 0.02 M metal ion worth of ascorbic acid. This is because of the availability of stoichiometric amounts of H ^+ ions from these reagents during dissolution. However, it was observed that rate of dissolution increases with increase in glycine concentration by keeping ascorbic acid concentration constant. We can observe about 70, 75, 86, 93 and 95% of Co ions dissolution takes place for 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 M respectively. When the concentration of glycine was 0.5 M, nearly all the Co ions dissolved from LiCoO2. As the glycine concentration increases from 0.1 to 0.5 M, the leaching efficiency also increases. During the leaching process, the lattice gets disturbed by the reduction of Co(III) to Co (II). Once the lattice is disturbed, the surrounding Co and Li ions are impelled from the LiCoO2 by hydrogen ion which leads to the disturbance in the lattice [20]. Once the lattice gets disturbed and leached to the solution, both Co and Li ions are expected as glycine complexes.

During the leaching, 0.02 M of ascorbic acid was added along with glycine to enhance the leaching reaction by reductive– complexing mechanism. On adding 0.02 M ascorbic acid, nearly all the Co(III) in LiCoO2 was further reduced to a soluble Co(II) which helps in complete dissolution. Previous studies of Li et al. [18,19,23,24,30] have clearly shown that the leaching efficiency was increased by adding reducing agent and also a similar behavior was observed in our previous reports [24,25]. Thus, it is advantageous to have a reducing agent along with glycine.

## 3.4. Effect of temperature and time on the leaching

The energy consumption of leaching will be a function of the working temperature and time. The effect of temperature and time on the leaching efficiency was studied by fixing the concentration of ascorbic acid (0.02 M) with glycine (0.1–0.5 M). There are many studies have shown the better leaching capacity for about 80 - 90 ^∘𝖢,, on the basis of these studies we have carried out leaching at 80 C [15,21,31]. Higher reaction temperature enhances the metal leaching, is due to the endothermicity of leachant dissociation, which translates to greater acid dissolution and increased reaction rates at elevated temperatures [19]. Above 90 ^∘ C, recovery of metal ions decreases because the acids begin to volatilize and the leachant solution becomes less.

## 3.5. Complexation and reduction of cobalt

Fig. 6 shows the complexation and reduction behavior of Co (III)–glycine to Co(II)–glycine. From the figure it is clear that, as the dissolution time increases, absorbance of the solution also increase. This increase in intensity of absorption is due to the complexation of Co ion with the glycine ligand. In Fig. 6 The maximum absorption () around 310 nm and 530 nm observed here are attributed to the Co(II)–glycine and Co(III)–glycine, respectively. The figure clearly indicates the reduction behaviour of Co(III)–glycine to Co(II)– glycine by ascorbic acid. The inset of Fig. 6 shows the UV–vis. Spectra of Co(III)–glycine and Co(II)–glycine complex in the absence of ascorbic acid. Here, the absorption peak for Co(III)–glycine and Co(II)–glycine are seen. In presence of ascorbic acid, the peak of Co(III)–glycine get reduced due to the reduction of Co(III)– to Co(II), which helps in making the reaction easy [32–34]. Therefore, we used ascorbic acid with glycine in leaching to increase the speed of reducing Co(III)–Co(II). Nevertheless, still we can observe the peak at 530 nm, which means still there are some Co(III) ions present in the solution which may be due to the fraction of Co(III)–glycine remaining because some amount of ascorbic acid is also utilized for deoxygenation of water in the dissolving medium. A similar behavior has been previously observed by us [20,24,25]. Here, the main reason for choosing glycine as complexing/leaching agent is due to its weak stability constant with metal ions unlike strong metal complexes such as Co(III)–EDTA and (log K = 41.4) and Fe (III)–EDTA (log K= 25.1) [35]. This week stability constant ofglycine with metal ions is beneficial for the successive precipitation of Co (II) ions as Co-oxalate. To the best of our knowledge, no reports are available on the Co–glycine complexes. Therefore we have recorded the UV–vis spectra for the dissolution mixture

## 3.6. Recovery of cobalt as cobalt oxalate

After 6 h of dissolution, on adding oxalic acid to the filtrate, Co (II)–glycine ions were precipitated as Co(II)–oxalate at room temperature immediately. The solid Co(II)–oxalate formed here was separated easily by filtration and washed with excess deionized water, dried in an oven. There was no Co remained in the filtrate. Therefore, a complete recovery of Co is achieved here. Fig. 7 shows the XRD pattern and Fig. 8 shows the FTIR spectrum of this solid powder sample. The XRD pattern of solid residues was confirmed to be well crystallized orthorhombic structured Co(II)– oxalate with space group of Cccm (JCPDS file: 25-0250) [15,20,31]. The FTIR band approximately3340 cm ^-1 has been assigned to O H stretching vibration and the band approximately1710 cm ^-1 has been assigned to CO stretching. The two peaks around 1310 cm1 and 1200 cm ^-1 are due to the presence of carbonyl group. The peak around 966 cm ^-1 could be ascribed to double bond stretching vibration of recovered compounds. The spectrum indicates O H group of the molecular water and the carbonyl group double bond group present in Co(II)– oxalate. These values are similar to the previous reports [20,21]. This cobalt oxalate be used as a Co precursor in preparing the LiCoO2 cathode material

## 4. Conclusion

A simple and environmental friendly hydrometallurgical route for the recovery of Co from spent LIBs has been developed by using mild, easily degradable organic acids. In this study we have determined the best conditions for Co leaching from spent LIBs (BL-5CANokia series). More than 95% ofCoions were extracted using 0.5 M glycine (chelating agent) and 0.02 M ascorbic acid (reductant) at 80 ^∘C for 6 h. UV–vis spectra of dissolved solution confirms the build–up of Co(II) glycine (≈ 310 nm) through the reduction of Co(III)–glycine (λ_ m a x ≈ 530 n m). The dissolved solution was subjected for selective precipitation of cobalt as Co–oxalate. There was a complete removal of Co from the dissolved solution.

## 2.2.2. Dissolution of LiCoO2 in mixture of glycine and ascorbic acid
The above cathode material (LiCoO2, 0.2: g) was subjected for chemical dissolution using mild organic acids, an aqueous mixture of glycine and ascorbic acid were taken in a three necked roundbottomed flask with volume of100 mL and the flask was placed in a water bath to control the reaction temperature during the leaching. The flask was fitted with vapor condenser and a magnetic stirrer. In the leaching process, the concentration of tartaric acid was varied (0.1–0.5 M) by keeping ascorbic acid concentration constant (0.02 M). After 6 h leaching at 80 ^∘𝖢,, the solution and insoluble residue were separated by filtration by using (0.2 mm) membrane filter paper and washed with distilled water, yielding a pink filtrate and a black residue.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.2. Effect of glycine concentration on leaching
The effect of glycine concentration on the leaching efficiency of waste LiCoO2 have been studied by varying concentration from
0.1 M to 0.5 M at temperature of 80 ^∘C for 6 h. The ascorbic acid (reductant) concentration used is 0.02 M and was kept constant. Fig. 4 shows the concentration dependency for leaching cobalt. The leaching efficiency of Co increases from 70% to 95% as the glycine concentration increases from 0.1 to 0.5 M. Therefore, here we used 0.5 M glycine with 0.02 M ascorbic acid for further leaching studies.
There are many studies on organic acid leaching. They have obtained more than 90% leaching of Co and about 100% leaching of Li in about 90–120 min by using 1.25 M citric acid [30], 1.5 M DL-malic acid [19], 1.0 M oxalic acid [31] along with H O as reducing agent. In all these studies they have used more concentrations to dissolve the metal ions completely, but in our case as reported in our previous study we have used mild concentrations; 0.1 M citric acid gives 80%, 0.4 M tartaric acid gives more than 90%, 0.1 M iminodiacetic acid gives 91% and 0.1 M maleic acid gives 97% Co and nearly 100% Li ions dissolution in the presence of 0.02 M ascorbic acid [20,24,25].

text_chunk.text:
## 3.3. Leaching with glycine and ascorbic acid
Fig. 5 shows the percentage of Co ions released from LiCoO in glycine and ascorbic acid (0.02 M) mixture at 80 C for 6 h. Here, in leaching of waste LiCoO we have tried the dissolution for stoichiometric glycine and ascorbic acid ratio with respect to the cathode material used. We used 0.02 M metal ion worth of LiCoO2 sample and was added to 100 mL water containing 0.1 - 0.5 N glycine and 0.02 M metal ion worth of ascorbic acid. This is because of the availability of stoichiometric amounts of H ^+ ions from these reagents during dissolution. However, it was observed that rate of dissolution increases with increase in glycine concentration by keeping ascorbic acid concentration constant. We can observe about 70, 75, 86, 93 and 95% of Co ions dissolution takes place for 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 M respectively. When the concentration of glycine was 0.5 M, nearly all the Co ions dissolved from LiCoO2. As the glycine concentration increases from 0.1 to 0.5 M, the leaching efficiency also increases. During the leaching process, the lattice gets disturbed by the reduction of Co(III) to Co (II). Once the lattice is disturbed, the surrounding Co and Li ions are impelled from the LiCoO2 by hydrogen ion which leads to the disturbance in the lattice [20]. Once the lattice gets disturbed and leached to the solution, both Co and Li ions are expected as glycine complexes.
During the leaching, 0.02 M of ascorbic acid was added along with glycine to enhance the leaching reaction by reductive– complexing mechanism. On adding 0.02 M ascorbic acid, nearly all the Co(III) in LiCoO2 was further reduced to a soluble Co(II) which helps in complete dissolution. Previous studies of Li et al. [18,19,23,24,30] have clearly shown that the leaching efficiency was increased by adding reducing agent and also a similar behavior was observed in our previous reports [24,25]. ## 3.4. Effect of temperature and time on the leaching
The energy consumption of leaching will be a function of the working temperature and time. The effect of temperature and time on the leaching efficiency was studied by fixing the concentration of ascorbic acid (0.02 M) with glycine (0.1–0.5 M). There are many studies have shown the better leaching capacity for about 80 - 90 ^∘𝖢,, on the basis of these studies we have carried out leaching at 80 C [15,21,31]. Higher reaction temperature enhances the metal leaching, is due to the endothermicity of leachant dissociation, which translates to greater acid dissolution and increased reaction rates at elevated temperatures [19]. Above 90 ^∘ C, recovery of metal ions decreases because the acids begin to volatilize and the leachant solution becomes less.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.6. Recovery of cobalt as cobalt oxalate
After 6 h of dissolution, on adding oxalic acid to the filtrate, Co (II)–glycine ions were precipitated as Co(II)–oxalate at room temperature immediately. The solid Co(II)–oxalate formed here was separated easily by filtration and washed with excess deionized water, dried in an oven. There was no Co remained in the filtrate. Therefore, a complete recovery of Co is achieved here. Fig. 7 shows the XRD pattern and Fig. 8 shows the FTIR spectrum of this solid powder sample. The XRD pattern of solid residues was confirmed to be well crystallized orthorhombic structured Co(II)– oxalate with space group of Cccm (JCPDS file: 25-0250) [15,20,31]. The FTIR band approximately3340 cm ^-1 has been assigned to O H stretching vibration and the band approximately1710 cm ^-1 has been assigned to CO stretching. The two peaks around 1310 cm1 and 1200 cm ^-1 are due to the presence of carbonyl group. The peak around 966 cm ^-1 could be ascribed to double bond stretching vibration of recovered compounds. The spectrum indicates O H group of the molecular water and the carbonyl group double bond group present in Co(II)– oxalate. These values are similar to the previous reports [20,21]. This cobalt oxalate be used as a Co precursor in preparing the LiCoO2 cathode material

final.content: Dissolve 0.2 g LiCoO2 cathode material in 100 mL aqueous mixture of glycine and ascorbic acid in a three-necked round-bottomed flask placed in a water bath at 80 °C for 6 h with magnetic stirring and vapor condensation. Vary glycine concentration from 0.1 to 0.5 M while keeping ascorbic acid concentration constant at 0.02 M. After leaching, separate solution and residue by filtration through 0.2 mm membrane filter and wash with distilled water, yielding pink filtrate and black residue.

settings.evidence_hint: The above cathode material (LiCoO2, 0.2 g) was subjected for chemical dissolution using mild organic acids, an aqueous mixture of glycine and ascorbic acid were taken in a three necked roundbottomed flask with volume of 100 mL and the flask was placed in a water bath to control the reaction temperature during the leaching. In the leaching process, the concentration of tartaric acid was varied (0.1–0.5 M) by keeping ascorbic acid concentration constant (0.02 M). After 6 h leaching at 80 °C, the solution and insoluble residue were separated by filtration.
